body.hook: Spanish is an official language in about 20 countries and is spoken by hundreds of millions of people, making it one of the most spoken languages in the world. Whether you're in Mexico City, Madrid or a Spanish-speaking neighbourhood in Calgary, it all starts with "¡Hola!"

study.title: ¡Mucho gusto!
study.question: How do I greet and introduce myself in Spanish?
study.passage:
Dialogue (read with a partner):
Sofía: ¡Hola! Buenos días.
Diego: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo te llamas?
Sofía: Me llamo Sofía. ¿Y tú?
Diego: Me llamo Diego. Mucho gusto.
Sofía: Igualmente. ¿Cómo estás?
Diego: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
Sofía: Más o menos. Tengo un examen hoy.
Diego: ¡Buena suerte! Hasta luego.
Sofía: ¡Adiós!
English support: Mucho gusto = Nice to meet you. Igualmente = Likewise. Muy bien = very well. Más o menos = so-so. Tengo un examen hoy = I have a test today. ¡Buena suerte! = Good luck!
Punctuation: Spanish questions and exclamations start with upside-down marks: ¿…? and ¡…!
Tú or usted? Use tú with friends and family; use usted with adults you don't know or to show respect: "¿Cómo se llama usted?" "¿Cómo está usted?"
Culture note: In many Latin American countries, friends often greet with one kiss on the cheek; in Spain, two is common. Handshakes are usual in formal settings.
study.source: Original dialogue written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to introduce myself with ser.

successCriteria: I can introduce myself with ser

body.hook: Spanish has two verbs for "to be." Today you'll meet the first one, ser, which you use to say who you are, where you're from and what you're like.

study.title: ¡Mucho gusto!
study.question: How do I introduce myself with ser?
study.passage:
Dialogue (read with a partner):
Lucía: ¡Hola! Me llamo Lucía. Soy de México. ¿Y tú? ¿De dónde eres?
Sam: Hola, Lucía. Me llamo Sam. Soy de Canadá. Soy de Calgary.
Lucía: ¡Mucho gusto, Sam!
Sam: Igualmente. ¿Cómo eres?
Lucía: Soy simpática y un poco tímida. ¿Y tú?
Sam: Soy alto y divertido.
Grammar: ser: yo soy, tú eres, él/ella/usted es.
Adjectives agree: -o for masculine, -a for feminine (alto, alta). Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant don't change (inteligente, popular).
Spanish punctuation: questions and exclamations start with upside-down marks: ¿…? ¡…!
Activity: "Speed introductions": in two lines, students introduce themselves in 30 seconds with name, origin and two adjectives, then move to the next partner.

body.objective: Students will be able to use numbers 0–20.
successCriteria: I can count from 0 to 20 in Spanish
I can say my age with tengo … años

body.hook: Phone numbers, ages, prices, scores: numbers are everywhere. Spanish numbers 0–20 are the building blocks for everything else, and they're used across more than 20 countries.

study.title: Los números
study.question: How do I count and use numbers 0–20 in Spanish?
study.passage:
Numbers (written for this lesson): 0 cero, 1 uno, 2 dos, 3 tres, 4 cuatro, 5 cinco, 6 seis, 7 siete, 8 ocho, 9 nueve, 10 diez, 11 once, 12 doce, 13 trece, 14 catorce, 15 quince, 16 dieciséis, 17 diecisiete, 18 dieciocho, 19 diecinueve, 20 veinte.
Pattern: 16–19 combine diez y + number into one word: dieciséis = diez y seis.
Age: Spanish uses tener (to have) for age: Tengo doce años (literally "I have twelve years"). ¿Cuántos años tienes?
Math: Dos más tres son cinco. Diez menos cuatro son seis.
Phone numbers are often read in pairs or single digits: cuatro, cero, tres…
Activities: 1. Count around the circle; skip multiples of 3 (say "¡olé!"). 2. Bingo with numbers 0–20. 3. Math race: partners solve spoken problems. 4. Survey ages: ¿Cuántos años tienes?
